title: Navigation for a nonprofit
excerpt: Label the menu with jobs donors and participants already name, and keep one path to give, join, or read on every page. Department names make them hunt.
alt: Curved library shelves packed with books, seen from a balcony, for a piece on a menu that helps people find the right volume.
caption: Shelves you can scan from above. A menu should be that legible. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should replace Get involved?
faqs.answer: The jobs hiding inside it. Volunteer, apply, give, or read the program, as separate labels when they are separate tasks. Get involved is a drawer. Visitors should not have to open it to learn which errand they are starting.

faqs.question: How do you serve participants and donors in one menu?
faqs.answer: With labels that do not force a person seeking help to wear a donor's task. Programs can lead. Give can be its own item. A single Support label that covers both makes the person in need translate, and many will leave instead.

faqs.question: What belongs in the footer instead of the bar?
faqs.answer: The slow and the legal. Address, privacy, jobs if you are hiring, older reports, and a login for people who already know to look. The bar stays on the tasks a new visitor has. A campaign can have a temporary line without earning a permanent slot.

markdown:
Nonprofit website navigation is a map of jobs, not a chart of the departments inside the building. A donor or a participant deciding whether the work is real should see labels they already use. One path should let them give, join, or read the program, and that path should be on every page. If the bar reads like a staff directory, the visitor has to do the translation. Many will not.

Build the menu from tasks. Find the program. See if it is for me. Read how to start. Give, if that is my role. Check the people and the report if I am still unsure. Labels that do not serve a task can live in the footer, or they can wait until a task exists.

## Words a donor and a participant already say

Listen to the voicemail and the front desk before you name the menu. People say the clinic, the pantry, volunteer, donate, the report, the address. They rarely say "our work," "get involved," or "resources." Use the public nouns. If two programs have names only the grant knows, this is the moment to give them public names and use those names everywhere.

Test a label by finishing "I need to…" "I need to see if the clinic is open." "I need to give to the food program." "I need to read the report." If the label cannot finish a sentence like that, it is a drawer. Open the drawer, promote the thing inside, and retire the drawer. "Get involved" is the most common drawer. It hides volunteering, hiring, and donating in one fog. Split the jobs that are actually different.

Keep the words stable. The menu, the program page heading, the intake form, and the way the phone is answered should match. A visitor who taps "Food bags" should land on a heading that says food bags. A synonym at the destination feels like a wrong turn even when the content is right. Small teams create synonyms by editing pages on different days. Write the list down and stick to it.

Order the bar by the visitor's decision. Programs first. The way to join or apply. The way to give. The report or the proof. About, for the reader who wants the people. Contact, if it is not already the action. News, if you must, at the end. Leading with a gala and a blog tells a participant that the site was arranged for supporters who already know you. Lead with the work, and supporters can still find the gift.

## One path that stays visible

Choose the primary action for this season and keep it visible in the header. If enrollment is open, the action might be apply. If you are in a giving campaign and enrollment is year-round and clear inside the programs, the action might be give. The other paths remain in the menu. The header should not shout three verbs at equal volume. A primary plus a quiet second is readable. A row of four identical buttons is a stall.

The verb has to match the page it opens. "Apply" should not dump a person into a donation form. "Give" should not open a volunteer orientation. These mix-ups happen when the button was copied from a template and the link was updated later, or never. Click the header from every template. Homepage, program, proof, article. The action should survive all of them.

On the page itself, repeat the relevant step. People arrive from a text message on a single program URL and never open the menu. The header is a promise for people who are browsing. The page is the promise for people who were sent. Both have to work. Navigation is not a substitute for a sentence at the end of a program block.

If "read the program" is one of your honest paths, make it a real destination. A program page with hours, place, cost, and boundary. Not a PDF from three years ago labeled brochure. If the report is the reading a donor needs, label it with the year. "Report" with no year will be assumed current, and if it is not, you have spent trust you needed.

## Separate doors when the audiences conflict

Participants and donors sometimes need different first doors. That does not require two websites. It requires labels that do not force a person seeking help to wear a donor's errand. "Get help" and "Give" can both be true. The harm is a single "Support" label that covers both, or a homepage hero that only speaks to funders while the menu hides the hours.

Language access belongs in the map when you truly offer it. A selector that leads to a full version in the languages you work in. A selector that leads to a homepage and then dead-ends in English is a broken door. Add it when the second version exists. Translate the labels, not just the body. A menu in English over a translated page tells the reader they are a guest in someone else's building.

A portal or a login for staff, board, or existing volunteers should be visually quiet. Those people know to look. A new participant should not meet a lock icon before they meet the program. Put the login in the footer or at the end of the menu. The same goes for a donor's "manage my gift" link. Useful, secondary, and worded as a human task.

## What stays out of the bar

Department names. Development, programs, operations, communications. Development survives only if you translate it into Give. The internal word is for the staff meeting. The menu is for everyone else. Advocacy, if it is a real program with a boundary, can be a program. As a top-level mood, it usually hides a blog.

A news river in the header. If you publish four notes a year, they do not deserve the second-most prominent label on the site. Park them in the footer or under About. If a note is truly urgent, a short dismissible line can carry it without a permanent promotion. Urgency that lives in the nav for months teaches people to ignore the nav.

Empty items from a template. Shop, forum, members, events, with nothing behind them, or with a single outdated flyer. Remove the item until the thing exists. A calendar with one event from last spring is an argument against your own reliability. The [W3C's WCAG overview](https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/) describes operable, navigable content as giving people ways to find what they need and to tell where they are. A menu of empty rooms does the opposite. It offers doors that do not open onto the work.

## Footer, search, and the phone

The footer holds the slow and the legal. Address in text, employer identification if you publish it, privacy, the jobs listing if hiring is real, the archive of reports by year. Repeat the primary action once for people who reach the bottom of a proof ready to move. Do not invent a new verb down there.

Search is optional. A small site with a search box often has labels that failed. Fix the labels first. Add search when the report archive or the program list is long enough to need it, and make sure a person can find "Tuesday clinic" and this year's report by the words they type. A search that only matches blog fluff will feel broken the first time a case worker uses it.

On a phone, keep the primary action outside the collapsed menu. Participants and donors both thumb these sites in transit. Hiding Apply or Give inside a hamburger icon, beside eight other items, demotes the path at the moment of decision. Inside the menu, use the same words and the same order as the wide screen. People switch devices. They forward links. The map should not change under them.

Give the rows room. Text labels, not mysterious icons. A menu icon can say "Menu." Focus states matter for people using a keyboard or assistive tech. These are ordinary quality bars. They are also how a navigation system stays usable when a plugin tries to be clever.

## Check the map with both audiences

Run two tasks with two people, or with one honest person playing straight. A participant: find out if the program is for you and how to start this week. A donor: find what a gift supports and where the latest numbers are. Watch the hesitations. Rename the label that caused the pause. Do not defend it. The pause is the finding.

Then open a program page directly, as if it arrived in a text, and ask both people how they would give or how they would find another program. Cross-links are where navigation fails after the homepage demo looked fine. Click every item on a phone. Confirm the heading at the destination. Confirm the header action is not covered by a banner or a chat bubble.

Write the menu in the project notes as a short list. When someone later wants to add a label for a campaign, ask which existing job it replaces, and when it will come out. A campaign can have a line on the homepage for a month. It rarely deserves a permanent slot beside the programs. The map stays stable so the people you serve can learn it.

Book [an intro call](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min) if you want the map built with the pages, rather than painted on afterward. Bring the words your front desk already uses. Those words are the menu. Hanabi designs and builds the site so the labels, the headings, and the action agree, and so you can change a program name without breaking three templates.

The labels will point at pictures, and the pictures will persuade or unsettle before the menu is even opened.
